learn.hook: Imagine asking a cat why it knocks things off the table — and getting an answer!
points: Doctor Dolittle is a character created by the English writer Hugh Lofting. He is a doctor who learns to talk with animals.
In the stories, his parrot Polynesia teaches him the language of animals, and he becomes a doctor for animals.
A doctor who treats animals is called a veterinarian, or vet.
Real animals communicate with sounds, movements and smells — honeybees even do a 'waggle dance' to show where flowers are.
Our own story below imagines a clinic where a bird helps a doctor understand animals.

example.q: Read: Dr Mehta's clinic in Pune was full of patients — but none of them were people! A goat with a sore hoof bleated, "Ma-a-a, my foot hurts!" Mynah, the clinic's chatty bird, flapped her wings and explained the problem to the doctor. "Thank you, Mynah," smiled Dr Mehta. "What would I do without my translator?" Why does Dr Mehta call Mynah his 'translator'?
steps: A translator changes words from one language into another.
The goat speaks in animal language; Mynah explains it to the doctor.
So Mynah does a translator's job.
example.answer: Because Mynah turns the animals' language into words the doctor can understand.

learn.reallife: Vets at animal hospitals and gaushalas read animals' body language — a limping goat or a cat that won't eat tells them something is wrong.

games.title: Dolittle and doctors
items: Doctor Dolittle was created by Hugh Lofting.
Hugh Lofting, an English writer, created him.
In the stories, Doctor Dolittle learns animal language from his parrot.
His parrot Polynesia teaches him.
A vet is a doctor who treats animals.
Vet is short for veterinarian.
Doctor Dolittle is a real doctor who lived in Pune.
He is an imaginary character in English storybooks.
Honeybees dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
This is called the waggle dance.

quiz.q: Who created the character Doctor Dolittle?
quiz.explain: Hugh Lofting, an English writer, wrote the Doctor Dolittle books.
quiz.mistake: Picks another well-known children's writer

quiz.q: In the Doctor Dolittle stories, who teaches the doctor the language of animals?
quiz.explain: His parrot Polynesia teaches him to understand animals. Jip and Chee-Chee are other animal friends.
quiz.mistake: Remembers other animals from the story but not the teacher

quiz.q: A doctor who treats animals is called a:
quiz.explain: Veterinarians (vets) treat animals. A paediatrician treats children; an optician deals with eyes and glasses.
quiz.mistake: Confuses different kinds of doctors

quiz.q: 'A goat with a sore hoof bleated, "Ma-a-a!"' The sound a goat makes is called a:
quiz.explain: Goats and sheep bleat. Horses neigh, elephants trumpet and owls hoot.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up animal sounds

quiz.q: 'Mynah flapped her wings and explained the problem to the doctor. "What would I do without my translator?" said Dr Mehta.' Why is Mynah called a translator?
options: She changes the animals' words into words the doctor understands
She sings songs for the patients
quiz.explain: A translator changes one language into another; Mynah turns animal talk into human words.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'translator'

quiz.q: What does 'translate' mean?
options: to change words from one language into another
quiz.explain: To translate is to put words into a different language.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the sound of the word

quiz.q: Which of these is a REAL way animals communicate?
options: A cat reads the morning newspaper.
A cow writes a letter to the farmer.
Honeybees dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
A goat speaks Hindi to the vet.
quiz.explain: The honeybee's waggle dance is a real way of sharing information. The others are fantasy.
quiz.mistake: Cannot tell real animal behaviour from fantasy

quiz.q: 'Dr Mehta's clinic was full of patients — but none of them were people!' Why is this line funny?
options: The doctor was not at work
We expect patients to be humans, but they are animals
quiz.explain: The surprise twist — the patients are animals — makes us smile.
quiz.mistake: Misses the surprise in the second half of the sentence

teach.ask: Gappu wants a doctor who understands chirps! Who is Doctor Dolittle and what is special about him?
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Doctor Dolittle would understand me perfectly!
teach.nudge: What is special about the way he talks to his patients?

learn.hook: A crocodile booking a train ticket to visit the dentist? That's imagination at work!
points: Fantasy describes things that cannot happen in real life, like talking animals or flying carpets.
Realistic writing describes things that could really happen.
Humour comes from surprise, silly situations, funny talk and exaggeration.
Exaggeration (hyperbole) makes something sound much bigger than it is: 'I've told you a million times!'
Word family: imagine (verb), imagination (noun), imaginary and imaginative (adjectives).

example.q: Is this fantasy or real, and why is it funny? 'The crocodile booked a train ticket to Chennai to see the dentist.'
steps: A huge-toothed crocodile worried about its teeth is a silly surprise.
example.answer: It is fantasy, and it is funny because of the silly, surprising situation.

learn.reallife: Cartoons, comics and funny ads on TV use talking animals and exaggeration to make us laugh.

games.title: Fantasy or real?
items: A tortoise flies a kite over Jaipur.
A camel reads the morning newspaper.
A crow becomes the class monitor.
An elephant plays the tabla at a wedding.
A hen lays an egg.
Bees collect nectar from flowers.
A puppy chews a slipper.
A cow eats grass.

quiz.q: Which sentence is fantasy?
options: A tiger opens a sweet shop in Kolkata.
A tiger rests in the shade.
quiz.explain: Tigers cannot run shops, so that sentence is fantasy.
quiz.mistake: Does not separate imagined events from real ones

quiz.q: Which sentence is realistic?
options: A dog teaches maths to puppies.
A dog barks at the postman.
A dog writes a poem about the moon.
A dog drives a bus to school.
quiz.explain: Dogs really do bark at strangers; the others cannot happen.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything with an animal is fantasy

quiz.q: 'This bag weighs a ton!' is an example of:
quiz.explain: A school bag doesn't really weigh a ton; the speaker is exaggerating for effect.
quiz.mistake: Takes the exaggeration as a comparison

quiz.q: Why do writers add humour to stories?
options: To entertain readers and make them smile
quiz.explain: Humour makes reading fun and keeps us interested.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about the writer's purpose

quiz.q: What does 'imaginary' mean?
quiz.explain: Something imaginary is made up, not real.
quiz.mistake: Confuses imaginary with real

quiz.q: Which word in this family is a noun: imagine, imagination, imaginary, imaginative?
quiz.explain: 'Imagination' names the ability; 'imagine' is a verb and the other two are adjectives.
quiz.mistake: Does not use word endings to find the word class

quiz.q: Which sentence uses exaggeration?
options: I'm so hungry I could eat a whole elephant!
quiz.explain: Nobody can eat an elephant — the speaker exaggerates to show great hunger.
quiz.mistake: Picks a plain fact

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'serious'?
quiz.explain: Grave, solemn and stern all mean serious; funny is the opposite.
quiz.mistake: Picks a synonym instead of an antonym

teach.ask: Gappu laughed at a story about a goat visiting the doctor. What makes such a story fantasy, and why is it funny?
teach.praise: Hee hee! Animals talking is fantasy, and the silly surprises make me giggle!
teach.nudge: Could it really happen? And what makes us laugh?

learn.hook: Quotation marks are like a speech bubble in a comic — they hold a speaker's exact words.
points: Direct speech gives the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks: Mynah said, "The goat is hurt."
The spoken words begin with a capital letter, and a comma, full stop, question mark or exclamation mark comes before the closing quotation mark.
Reported (indirect) speech tells what someone said without quotation marks, often using 'that': Mynah said that the goat was hurt.
When the reporting verb is in the past (said), the tense usually moves back: am/is → was, can → could, will → would, like → liked.
Pronouns change to fit: Rohan said, "I am tired." → Rohan said that he was tired. Universal truths stay in the present tense.

example.q: Change to reported speech: Rohan said, "I can help the goat."
steps: Remove the quotation marks and add 'that'.
'can' moves back to 'could' because 'said' is past.
example.answer: Rohan said that he could help the goat.

learn.reallife: News reports, comics and your diary use both — direct speech for exact words, reported speech to retell them.

items.text: He said, "I am sleepy." → He said that he ___ sleepy.
She said, "I can run fast." → She said that she ___ run fast.
They said, "We will come." → They said that they ___ come.
Raju said, "I like dogs." → Raju said that he ___ dogs.

games.title: Build the sentence
games.prompt: Arrange to make correct direct speech
items: The vet said,
"Your dog
will be
fine soon."

quiz.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Priya said, The parrot can talk.
quiz.explain: A comma after 'said', quotation marks around the exact words, a capital T, and the full stop inside the closing marks.
quiz.mistake: Puts quotation marks around the wrong words or forgets the capital letter

quiz.q: Change to reported speech: Arun said, "I am hungry."
options: Arun says that I was hungry.
Arun said that he were hungry.
Arun said that he was hungry.
Arun said that I am hungry.
quiz.explain: 'I' becomes 'he' and 'am' moves back to 'was'.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change the pronoun or the tense

quiz.q: In reported speech after 'said', 'will' usually changes to:
quiz.explain: The past form of 'will' is 'would'.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the past form of the modal

quiz.q: Which sentence is in direct speech?
options: Meena said that she loved mangoes.
quiz.explain: Direct speech shows the exact words inside quotation marks.
quiz.mistake: Confuses reported speech with direct speech

quiz.q: What do quotation marks show?
options: the title of a chapter only
quiz.explain: Quotation marks (inverted commas) go around a speaker's exact words.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the main use of quotation marks

quiz.q: Change to reported speech: Sita said, "I can swim."
options: Sita said that she could swam.
Sita said that she can swims.
Sita said that she could swim.
Sita said that I could swim.
quiz.explain: 'I' becomes 'she', and 'can' becomes 'could' followed by the base verb 'swim'.
quiz.mistake: Changes the main verb instead of the modal

quiz.q: Change to reported speech: The teacher said, "The Earth goes around the Sun."
options: The teacher said that the Earth is going around the Sun.
The teacher said that the Earth went around the Sun yesterday.
The teacher said that the Earth goes around the Sun.
The teacher said that the Earth had gone around the Sun.
quiz.explain: A universal truth stays in the simple present even in reported speech.
quiz.mistake: Changes the tense of a universal truth

quiz.q: Ravi asked, "Can animals talk" — where should the question mark go?
quiz.explain: The question mark belongs to the spoken question, so it goes inside: Ravi asked, "Can animals talk?"
quiz.mistake: Places the question mark outside the quotation marks

teach.ask: Gappu wrote: Mynah said I am hungry. What is missing in direct speech, and how do we report it?
teach.praise: So it's: Mynah said, "I am hungry." Or: Mynah said that she was hungry. Neat!
teach.nudge: Where do the quotation marks and comma go? And how would we report it with 'that'?
